title: Counting the Omer
hook: Jews count seven weeks of days from Passover to Shavuot, some giving each day a quality

segments.voice: Yesterday, Musar: character work, practicing one trait at a time. Your line was one trait. Did the trait you chose show up anywhere, and did you write your line? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

During Passover, in Jewish homes and synagogues, someone says a blessing in the evening and then one short sentence: today is one day of the Omer. The next evening: today is two days of the Omer. Then three. Then four. Night after night, a number said out loud, and nothing else to do. No meal attached to it, no special clothes. Just the number, growing, all the way to the festival of Shavuot. It's an odd kind of practice to keep up for weeks. And yet it has its own blessing, its own rules, and an old question about what happens if you forget. Today's word is that count.
screen: `TODAY IS ONE DAY OF THE OMER.` → `NIGHT AFTER NIGHT, A NUMBER.` → `ALL THE WAY TO SHAVUOT.`

segments.voice: The count comes straight from the Torah. Leviticus says, in the King James wording: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete." That sheaf is the omer, an offering of new grain from the harvest. Seven weeks of days, counted one by one, and then a festival: Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks. Jewish tradition ties the two ends together. Passover remembers leaving Egypt. Shavuot, tradition says, remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai. So the count walks a road, from being set free to being given something to live by. And notice which way it runs. It's a count up, not a countdown. A countdown treats the days in between as waiting room. A count up adds each day to the total, so that every one of them is kept. Over time a second layer grew around the count. Some Jews, following the kabbalists, give each of the seven weeks a quality, starting with chesed, loving-kindness, and give each day within the week a shade of those qualities. Loving-kindness within loving-kindness. Strength within loving-kindness. For one day, a person looks at that single shade of themselves. Then the rabbis add a very human question: what about someone who forgets to count for a whole day? One well-known ruling says keep counting, but without the blessing. The count is too important to drop. A missed night doesn't send anyone back to the start.
screen: `THE SHEAF, AND SEVEN WEEKS.` · `FROM FREEDOM TO SINAI.` · `A COUNT UP, NOT A COUNTDOWN.` · `A QUALITY FOR EACH DAY.` · then, large: `SEVEN SABBATHS SHALL BE COMPLETE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count one quality today. Settle, and let the breath slow. Take the quality the count begins with, loving-kindness, and look for it in your last day. Where did kindness come easily? Where did it stall, or go missing? Don't grade yourself. Just look. Then say quietly inside, the way a counter would: today is one. One day of noticing one quality. If you pray, you can hold that day before God. If you don't, just hold it in your attention, breath by breath. The bell holds the time.
Counting the Omer. Seven weeks of days, counted aloud one by one from Passover to Shavuot, and for some, a quality for every day. Today's word.

Your line: count the days. Today, begin a small count of your own: one thing you'll notice each day this week. Say the number to yourself tonight, and keep going tomorrow. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Jews who keep the count say a blessing each evening from the second night of Passover and then state the day's number of the Omer until Shavuot; some also reflect on a kabbalistic quality assigned to that day.

notes: Confirm KJV wording of Leviticus 23:15 as quoted.

The omer is described as 'an offering of new grain from the harvest' (Lev 23:10: 'a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest'); the rabbinic identification as barley is not stated in the voice. The original-game note calls omer 'a sheaf, and a measure of grain'; confirm.
Shavuot as the remembrance of the giving of the Torah is framed as 'tradition says' (it is not stated in the Torah). Confirm.

The kabbalistic scheme (seven weeks = seven lower sefirot, starting with chesed; each day a sefirah within a sefirah) is attributed to 'some Jews, following the kabbalists'. Confirm 'strength within loving-kindness' (gevurah she-bechesed) as day two.
Missed-day ruling: Shulchan Aruch OC 489:8 (one who missed a whole day continues counting without a blessing); presented as 'one well-known ruling' since opinions differ. Confirm.
howItsDone says the count begins on the second night of Passover (rabbinic reading of 'the morrow after the sabbath'); this is in howItsDone only, not the voice. Confirm.
Index hook says forty-nine days; the script says 'seven weeks of days' following the cited text ('seven sabbaths shall be complete').
